paragraphs.heading: A ceiling on inner products
paragraphs.text: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, also called the Cauchy–Bunyakovsky–Schwarz inequality, puts an upper limit on the inner product of two vectors. It says the absolute value of that inner product can be no bigger than the product of the two vectors' norms. It is counted among the most important and most widely used inequalities in mathematics. Since inner products can stand for finite sums, infinite series or integrals, the one statement covers all three.

paragraphs.heading: Who found it
paragraphs.text: Augustin-Louis Cauchy published the version for sums in 1821. The matching inequality for integrals was published by Viktor Bunyakovsky in 1859 and by Hermann Schwarz in 1888. Schwarz also gave the modern proof of that integral version.

paragraphs.heading: Picture it in the plane
paragraphs.text: In the flat plane ℝ², the inner product is the ordinary dot product. There the inequality says (‖𝐮‖‖𝐯‖cos θ)² can be at most ‖𝐮‖²‖𝐯‖², with θ standing for the angle that separates the two vectors. This may be the easiest form to grasp: the square of a cosine is never more than 1, and it reaches 1 when the vectors point the same way or opposite ways.

paragraphs.heading: When the two sides match
paragraphs.text: In coordinates, with 𝐮 = (u₁, u₂) and 𝐯 = (v₁, v₂), the inequality reads (u₁v₁ + u₂v₂)² ≤ (u₁² + u₂²)(v₁² + v₂²). The two sides are equal only if the vectors line up in the same or opposite directions, or one of them is the zero vector. In general, the two sides match exactly when the vectors are linearly dependent.

paragraphs.heading: Angles in any space
paragraphs.text: One payoff is a meaning for the angle between two vectors in any real inner-product space. You define cos θ_𝐮𝐯 = (⟨𝐮, 𝐯⟩)/‖𝐮‖‖𝐯‖, and Cauchy–Schwarz shows the right-hand side always lies between −1 and 1, so the definition makes sense. That supports the view that real Hilbert spaces are simply generalizations of Euclidean space.

paragraphs.heading: Where it gets used
paragraphs.text: The inequality has many uses. It proves that the inner product is a continuous function, and it can prove the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators in finite dimensions. In probability, defining the inner product of two random variables as the expectation of their product turns it into |E (XY)| ² ≤ E (X²)E (Y²). In graph theory it proves Mantel's theorem: a graph on n vertices with no triangles has at most ⌊1/4n²⌋ edges.
